concepts.title: Scarcity, Choice and Basic Economic Activities
concepts.definition: Every decision-making unit - a family, a weaver, a teacher - holds only a little of what it needs, so limited means force a selection among competing wants; production, exchange and consumption are the everyday activities through which people cope with this squeeze.
concepts.key_idea: Because no one owns endless resources, having more of one thing always means having less of another.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec201.txt, section 1.1, family farm and weaver examples, pages 1-3
question_patterns: why does limited means force a choice between competing wants for every household
how do families and workers cope when their resources fall short of their needs
name the basic economic activities people perform in daily life
what is the economic problem that every decision-making unit faces
explain with an example how obtaining one good means giving up another
why can no individual possess everything she wishes to consume

solution_steps.explain: Each unit possesses only a few of the many things it needs, so wants outrun means by definition.
With capped resources, gaining more of one good requires surrendering some of another - a trade-off.
Units produce with what they hold, exchange the surplus for the rest, and consume the result - the loop of basic economic life.

concepts.title: Central Problems: What, How and For Whom to Produce
concepts.definition: Scarce resources with rival uses oblige every society to settle which goods to make and in what amounts, which techniques and resource mixes to employ, and how the finished output is shared among its members.
concepts.key_idea: Scarcity breeds choice, and choice splits into three decisions every economy must make.
question_patterns: which three decisions about output techniques and sharing must every society settle
why does scarcity give rise to the problem of choice among rival uses
give examples of choices involved in deciding the composition of output
what does choosing a production technique mean in practice
how is the question of output sharing a problem of distribution
should basic education and health be free for all - which central problem does this raise

solution_steps.explain: Decide quantities of food, clothing, defence, education and investment goods to be produced.
Decide how much labour versus machinery, and which technology, goes into each good.
Decide who receives how much of the output, including whether minimum consumption is guaranteed to all.

concepts.title: Production Possibility Set and the Frontier
concepts.definition: With fixed resources and known technology an economy can turn out many mixes of two goods; the set of all attainable mixes is the production possibility set, and the boundary curve through the fully-employed mixes is the production possibility frontier.
concepts.formula: frontier = maximum_mixes_of(good_a, good_b) under full resource employment
concepts.key_idea: Points on the curve exhaust resources; points inside signal idle or wasted capacity.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec201.txt, section 1.2, corn-cotton Table 1.1 and figure, pages 4-5
question_patterns: define the collection of attainable output mixes of an economy
what does the curve of maximum output combinations show
corn and cotton possibilities are tabulated, draw the frontier
why does a point below the curve mean underemployment or waste
can an economy operate beyond its frontier with given resources
what information fixes the shape of the attainable-output curve

solution_steps.explain: Given the total resource stock and current knowledge, list every mix of the two goods that can be produced.
Mixes produced when all resources are employed form the frontier; each point is a maximum of one good for the other held.
On the curve means efficient full employment, inside means slack or waste, outside is unattainable with present means.

concepts.title: Opportunity Cost along the Frontier
concepts.definition: Moving along the frontier to gain a unit of one good obliges the economy to give up some of the other; the amount of the second good sacrificed per unit gained is the opportunity cost, also called the economic cost.
concepts.key_idea: Every extra unit has a price in forgone alternatives, and that price is the sacrifice ratio along the frontier.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec201.txt, section 1.2, opportunity cost paragraph after Table 1.1, page 5
question_patterns: compute the sacrifice ratio when output shifts from one frontier point to another
moving from 2 units of corn and 7 of cotton to 3 corn and 4 cotton, what is given up per corn gained
define opportunity cost and explain why it is called the economic cost
why does producing more of one good force the economy to give up another
find what society sacrifices for an extra unit chosen from a possibilities table
how does the idea of forgone alternatives apply to a single person as well

solution_steps.explain: Subtract the new quantity of the other good from its old quantity to find how much was surrendered.
The surrendered amount per extra unit of the chosen good is the opportunity cost of that move.

worked_examples.question: Using Opportunity Cost along the Frontier, compute the result for initial_output_of_other_good = 3, final_output_of_other_good = 3, extra_units_of_chosen_good = 3.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Measure the sacrifice: quantity_lost_of_other_good = initial_output_of_other_good - final_output_of_other_good = 0.0 Step 2: Divide by the gain: opportunity_cost = quantity_lost_of_other_good / extra_units_of_chosen_good = 0.0 Final result: 0.0

worked_examples.question: Using Opportunity Cost along the Frontier, compute the result for initial_output_of_other_good = 4, final_output_of_other_good = 4, extra_units_of_chosen_good = 4.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Measure the sacrifice: quantity_lost_of_other_good = initial_output_of_other_good - final_output_of_other_good = 0.0 Step 2: Divide by the gain: opportunity_cost = quantity_lost_of_other_good / extra_units_of_chosen_good = 0.0 Final result: 0.0

concepts.title: Centrally Planned Economy
concepts.definition: In a centrally planned economy a central authority - the government - takes all major decisions about production, exchange and consumption, steering resources toward goals it judges good for society, such as adequate schooling or an equitable output share.
concepts.key_idea: One planner replaces the market: the state decides the allocation and the distribution directly.
question_patterns: who settles the major economic questions in a centrally planned system
how does a central authority correct an unequal share of output
when would the state itself start producing a good like health service
describe how production and exchange are organised without markets
give an instance of planning decisions aimed at social welfare
what powers does the government hold in a planned economy

solution_steps.explain: The government or central authority owns the choices of what, how and for whom.
Planning pursues allocations and distributions regarded as desirable for society, not private profit.
The state may induce or itself produce under-supplied goods and redistribute output where survival is at stake.

concepts.title: Market Economy and Coordination by Prices
concepts.definition: A market is the set of arrangements letting buyers and sellers deal freely, whether face to face or over distance; when buyers want more of a good its price rises, signalling producers to expand, so prices alone coordinate the plans of millions of dispersed agents.
concepts.key_idea: Prices carry information about society's valuation, and chasing them quietly solves what and how much to produce.
question_patterns: how do rising and falling prices coordinate decisions in a market system
define a market as economists use the term
must buyers and sellers meet in one place for a market to exist
explain the signal a price increase sends to producers
through what arrangement do free exchanges between agents take place
who answers the question of how much to produce in a market system

solution_steps.explain: A market is the institutional space - physical or virtual - where agents freely trade endowments and products.
Excess demand lifts the price, telling producers society wants more; excess supply does the reverse.
Responding to prices, independent agents end up producing roughly what society values, without any central command.

concepts.title: Mixed Economy in Practice
concepts.definition: Real-world economies blend the two poles: markets conduct most activity while the government takes important decisions, and systems differ only in how large the state's role is - minimal in the United States, sweeping in twentieth-century China, historically large in India.
concepts.key_idea: Between laissez-faire and full planning lies a spectrum, and every actual economy sits somewhere on it.
question_patterns: why are all actual economies called mixed
how do countries differ in the share of decisions left to government
compare the government's economic role in the United States China and India
give examples of decisions a state takes even in a market-led economy
what determines where an economy sits between market and plan
has the government's role in the Indian economy grown or shrunk recently

solution_steps.explain: Markets handle most production and exchange; the government still takes key allocation and distribution decisions.
The state's weight ranges from minimal in the USA to dominant in Mao-era China, with India historically state-heavy.
India has pared down the government's economic role considerably in recent decades.

concepts.title: Positive versus Normative Economic Analysis
concepts.definition: Positive analysis describes how an economic mechanism actually works and what outcomes it yields, while normative analysis passes judgement on whether those outcomes are desirable; the two strands interlock, since judging requires understanding.
concepts.key_idea: Description comes before evaluation, but sound evaluation feeds back into what we choose to describe.
question_patterns: separate statements of fact from statements of value in economics
what does positive economic analysis try to establish
what question does normative economics set out to answer
classify a claim about a mechanism's working versus its desirability
why can the two kinds of analysis not be fully separated
give one positive and one normative statement about a market outcome

solution_steps.explain: A claim about how a mechanism functions is positive; a claim about whether the result is good is normative.
Analysis of functioning precedes evaluation of desirability for each alternative mechanism.
Valuing outcomes needs understanding of mechanisms and vice versa, so the boundary stays blurred.

concepts.title: Microeconomics and Macroeconomics as Branches
concepts.definition: Microeconomics follows individual agents in single markets to see how each good's price and quantity emerge, while macroeconomics steps back to aggregate totals - output, employment and the general price level - and how they are set and how they move.
concepts.key_idea: One branch zooms to a market, the other zooms out to the whole economy's totals.
question_patterns: contrast the study of single markets with the study of economy-wide totals
which questions about total output and jobs belong to the aggregate branch
what does the individual-agent branch try to determine
sort topics like a good's price and the general price level into their branches
why are output employment and the price level called aggregate measures
state the subject matter of each broad branch of economics

solution_steps.explain: Micro looks at consumers and producers in one commodity market; macro looks at economy-wide aggregates.
Micro asks how a good's price and quantity form; macro asks how total output, employment and prices are determined and why they change.
Questions naming totals or the whole economy go to macro; those naming one good or agent go to micro.
